findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add tests/unit/test_rp04_s4_llm_runtime.py to Scope, and say where the subclass is defined so that the `BedrockProvider` monkeypatch at line 110 (and the `_Stub` in test_bedrock_provider.py:561) still works, re-derived with `find_referencing_symbols` plus a string grep for "BedrockProvider".
evidence: Plan Scope lists only `src/rebar/llm/bedrock_model.py` and `tests/unit/test_bedrock_provider.py`
tests/unit/test_rp04_s4_llm_runtime.py:110: `monkeypatch.setattr(pai_bedrock, "BedrockProvider", lambda **kw: SimpleNamespace(**kw))`
src/rebar/llm/bedrock_model.py:56: `from pydantic_ai.providers.bedrock import BedrockProvider` (imported inside the function, so it picks up the monkeypatched object)
findings.finding: `BedrockProvider`, the symbol the fix subclasses, is replaced by name with a lambda in tests/unit/test_rp04_s4_llm_runtime.py:110. The plan's Scope leaves that file out. `build_bedrock_provider` imports `BedrockProvider` lazily inside the function (bedrock_model.py:56). If the subclass is defined after that import, under this monkeypatch it becomes `class _X(<lambda>)`, which raises TypeError, so `test_injected_session...` breaks. If the subclass is instead defined at module level, the stub is bypassed and the module's lazy-import rule (module docstring; pyproject.toml:147) is broken.
scenarios: tests/unit/test_rp04_s4_llm_runtime.py:108-119: the injected-session test calls `session.provider_factory("bedrock")`, which goes through `build_bedrock_provider`. Subclassing the patched lambda raises TypeError, and `make verify` (the last AC) fails.

If the subclass is moved to module level to avoid that, test_rp04_s4 no longer checks the stub, and `rebar.llm.bedrock_model` imports pydantic_ai's bedrock module (and botocore) eagerly. That breaks the optional-dependency boundary that the bedrock_provider capability check relies on.
findings.suggested_fix: Define the subclass inside `build_bedrock_provider` with a guard (subclass only when `isinstance(BedrockProvider, type)`), or wrap with a factory that leaves non-class stubs alone. Alternatively, update test_rp04_s4_llm_runtime.py:110 to patch with a class, and add that file to Scope.

findings.finding: The wrap changes behavior for unknown Bedrock vendor prefixes as well as meta. The plan does not analyse or test the downstream effect of that change. Unknown vendors previously resolved `model_profile` to `None`, so pydantic-ai fell back to a plain profile and capabilities classified them as `none` style. After the wrap they become `BedrockModelProfile.from_profile(DEFAULT_PROFILE)`, which exposes `bedrock_supports_prompt_caching`, so `_capabilities_from_profile` will now classify them `bedrock` style. The Capability classification section measures this flip only for meta. The tests assert only that unknown vendors resolve to a `BedrockModelProfile`, not their capabilities or the absence of `cachePoint`. The plan also does not say whether any existing test pins meta or unknown vendors to `none` style. Such a test would need modifying, yet the scope lists only `bedrock_model.py` and `test_bedrock_provider.py`.
scenarios: An operator uses a new or unknown Bedrock vendor prefix. Its `prompt_cache_style` silently flips from `none` to `bedrock`, and `cache_settings_for` begins emitting bedrock cache settings that nothing tested for that profile.
An existing capabilities unit test asserts meta or unknown vendors are `none` style. It fails under `make verify` and forces an unplanned edit outside the declared scope.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the classification test parametric over meta and an unknown vendor prefix. Assert `bedrock` style, `native_structured_output=False`, and no `cachePoint` in the agentic Converse request for both. Add one line to the Capability classification section covering unknown vendors. Grep the existing tests for meta/unknown `none`-style assertions and list any hit in Scope.

findings.finding: The Approach doesn't say where the new `BedrockModelProfile` import and the `BedrockProvider` subclass go. BedrockModelProfile lives in `pydantic_ai.models.bedrock`, which imports botocore when it loads. capabilities.py imports `rebar.llm.bedrock_model` on the capability path that always runs (to get resolve_bedrock_region). If the subclass or the import is put at module level, that path will need botocore, and boto3 is absent in CI. findings.finding: The approach claims that, for meta, 'a strict tool is sent without `strict`, as pydantic-ai main does'. No test asserts the shape of the outgoing Converse toolSpec, so the regression could pass with `strict` still present or the tool silently dropped.
scenarios: A future pydantic-ai change emits `strict` for meta and Bedrock rejects it live, while the unit tests stay green.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the tool-using-turn test to inspect the scripted client's first captured `converse` kwargs. Assert that the tool name is present in `toolConfig['tools'][*]['toolSpec']['name']` and that `'strict' not in toolSpec`.

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
